anchor: ## 1. The data
caption: Figure 0.1 — The three species in the dataset. In an iris the three drooping outer parts are the sepals and the three smaller upright inner parts are the petals; the four measurements in the table are the length and width of each. Photos from Wikimedia Commons: Radomil (CC BY-SA 3.0), Danielle Langlois (CC BY-SA 3.0) and Frank Mayfield (CC BY-SA 2.0), cropped and resized.
alt: Three photographs of iris flowers side by side, labelled Iris setosa, Iris versicolor and Iris virginica.

anchor: The split is random, but the seed fixes it
caption: Figure 0.2 — The 150 flowers split into 112 for training and 38 for testing. Filled squares are the test flowers. Because of `stratify=y`, each species appears in both sets in the same proportion: 12, 13 and 13 of each species are in the test set.
alt: Three rows of 50 squares, one row per species, with the 38 test flowers filled in and the rest outlined.

anchor: ## The pattern to take away
caption: Figure 0.4 — The five-step experiment chain that every later session follows: split, baseline, fit, evaluate, read the errors. A small version of this strip opens each session with that session's step highlighted.
alt: Five boxes in a row, joined by arrows: split, baseline, fit, evaluate, read the errors.

anchor: ## Where the ideas in this course came from
caption: Figure 0.5 — The history table as a timeline. Most of the methods in the course are older than they look; the labels near the line give the session that builds on each.
alt: A horizontal timeline from 1936 to 2022 with ten events marked, each labelled with the session that builds on it.

anchor: The rule scores 0.964 on the training flowers
caption: Figure 0.3 — The hand-written rule. Left: the two questions, with how many of the 112 training flowers reach each answer. Right: the same two thresholds drawn on the training flowers' petals; circled flowers are the ones the rule gets wrong.
alt: A two-question flowchart (petal length under 2.5 cm, then petal width under 1.75 cm) beside a scatter of the training flowers with a vertical line at 2.5 cm and a horizontal line at 1.75 cm.

anchor: For each species $k$ the model forms a score
caption: Figure 0.6 — What the model computes for one test flower (the first one it gets wrong). The four rescaled measurements are multiplied by each species' weights and added to its intercept, giving three scores; softmax turns the scores into probabilities.
alt: Four rescaled measurements, a three-by-four grid of fitted weights, three scores and three probabilities for one test flower, with the largest probability on the wrong species.

anchor: ## 1. What is one row?
caption: Figure 1.1 — One row of the table, the first student. Most columns are features the model may read; `student_id` only labels the row, and `passed` is the target the model will try to predict.
alt: A table row split into seven labelled cells: student_id marked as not a feature, three numeric and two category features, and the passed column marked as the target.

anchor: One row appears twice
caption: Figure 1.2 — Why a duplicate matters. Student S0025 sits at positions 25 and 500 with identical values. If a random split puts one copy in the training set and the other in the test set, the model is tested on a row it has already seen.
alt: Two identical rows for student S0025, at positions 25 and 500; a random split sends one to the training set and one to the test set.

anchor: ## 5. Which features separate the outcomes?
caption: Figure 1.5 — The pass rate among students at the two ends of each feature. Many more of those who studied for a long time, or had a high previous grade, passed than of those at the other end; attendance separates the ends least.
alt: Three pairs of bars, one pair per feature, showing the share who passed among students at the low end and the high end: study hours 32% and 93%, previous grade 28% and 92%, attendance 40% and 74%.

anchor: Two columns have gaps: 22 students have no
caption: Figure 1.3 — Where the gaps are: one column per row of the picture, one tick per student, dark where the value is missing. The 22 missing grades and the 15 missing departments fall on different students and show no pattern.
alt: A strip chart with one line per column and 500 positions along it; dark ticks mark the 22 missing previous grades and the 15 missing departments, scattered with no visible pattern.

anchor: The sample of 101 Business students is small
caption: Figure 1.6 — The pass rate per department with a 95% interval (the rate plus or minus two standard errors). Business has the fewest students, so its interval is the widest: the true Business rate could plausibly sit several points either side of 52.5%.
alt: Three dots with vertical interval bars: CS 68.7%, Engineering 59.3% and Business 52.5% pass rate, the Business bar the longest.

anchor: Each plot compares the students who passed
caption: Figure 1.4 — The same question in finer steps: the pass rate in five equal-count bands of study hours and of previous grade (about 100 students in each band). The rate climbs steadily, not in a jump at one threshold.
alt: Two small bar charts of pass rate in five bands: study hours rises from about a third to over 90 percent, previous grade likewise.

anchor: If $Y=X^2$ and $X$ is spread evenly around zero
caption: Figure 1.8 — A relationship the correlation cannot see. Y is exactly X squared, so X determines Y completely, yet Pearson's r is close to zero: the points go up on one side and down on the other. (Constructed example, 200 points.)
alt: A U-shaped curve of points, Y equal to X squared, with the printed correlation near zero.

anchor: Each case calls for a different treatment
caption: Figure 1.7 — The three kinds of missing value on one constructed set of 400 students. Dark points are kept, pale ones are hidden. When the gap depends on the hidden value itself (right), the kept students are no longer a fair sample: their average is too high.
alt: Three scatter plots of study hours against previous grade, hiding grades completely at random, depending on a visible column, and depending on the grade itself; the last shows a higher average among the kept students.

anchor: ## 3. Numbers: fill the gaps, then rescale
caption: Figure 2.1 — `fit` and `transform`. The medians are learned from the 375 training rows only; the same numbers are then applied to the training rows and the 125 test rows.
alt: Training rows feed a box of learned numbers (three medians) through an arrow labelled fit; transform arrows carry those numbers to both the training and the test rows.

anchor: ## 3. Numbers: fill the gaps, then rescale
caption: Figure 2.2 — The right order and the wrong order. Fitting before the split lets the test rows shape the numbers the model sees. In the right order the scaled test columns are not centred on zero (their means are -0.114, 0.264 and -0.092) because they use the training numbers.
alt: Two columns of three steps. Right: split, fit on training rows, transform both sets. Wrong: fit on all rows, then split, with information leaking from the test rows into the fitted numbers.

anchor: ## 4. Categories: fill the gaps, then one-hot encode
caption: Figure 2.3 — One-hot encoding. Each department becomes its own 0/1 column, so no department is placed between two others. Numbering the departments 0, 1, 2 would put them on a line and make Engineering look like the middle of CS and Business.
alt: Left, four rows of department names; right, the same rows as three columns of zeros and ones, one column per department. Below, a number line placing the departments at 0, 1 and 2, labelled as the wrong choice.

anchor: ## 5. One pipeline, one object
caption: Figure 2.4 — The structure of the pipeline. A ColumnTransformer sends the numeric columns through an imputer and a scaler and the category columns through an imputer and a one-hot encoder; the results are joined and passed to the classifier.
alt: Two branches of boxes: numeric columns through impute and scale, category columns through impute and one-hot encode, joined into one table that feeds a logistic regression classifier.

anchor: ## 6. How much should one split be trusted?
caption: Figure 2.5 — Five-fold cross-validation. Each fold holds back a different fifth of the students and scores the model on it. The five accuracies spread from 0.72 to 0.85 around a mean of 0.792; the single test split (0.832) happens to fall on the easier side.
alt: Left, a grid of five rows with one cell highlighted in each, showing which fifth is held out in each fold. Right, the five fold accuracies as dots with their mean and the single test-split accuracy marked.

anchor: ## 7. Leakage: the model that looks perfect
caption: Figure 2.6 — Leakage as a timeline. The features exist when the student enrols, before the prediction is needed. The certificate is issued after the outcome is known, so it matches the target exactly (312 Yes among those who passed, 188 No among those who failed) and cannot be used to predict it.
alt: A timeline from enrolment to certificate with the moment the prediction is needed marked in the middle. Columns known before that moment are labelled safe; the certificate, issued afterwards, is labelled as leaking the answer.

anchor: The line cuts through both moons
caption: Figure 3.1 — How each model reaches an answer for one test point (the star, the one where the k-NN vote is closest). Logistic regression: which side of a line. k-NN: the vote of the 17 circled nearest training points. Tree: which of the first rectangles. Forest: how many of its 200 trees vote for each class.
alt: Four panels of the two half-moons: a straight dividing line; a star with its 17 nearest training points circled; the tree's first three splits drawn as lines; and a bar chart of how the 200 trees of the forest voted for the star point.

anchor: Without scaling the test accuracy drops from 0.919 to 0.705
caption: Figure 3.2 — The same test point (the star) and its 17 nearest training points, in three versions of the data. Left: the original features. Middle: feature 1 multiplied by 1,000, so the neighbours are simply the points with the closest feature 1, a thin slab that ignores feature 2. Right: after StandardScaler, the neighbourhood is local again.
alt: Three scatter plots with a star and 17 circled neighbours: a compact round neighbourhood on the original data, a tall thin vertical slab of neighbours on the stretched data, and a compact neighbourhood again after scaling.

anchor: Both look excellent by accuracy.
caption: Figure 4.1 — The 5000 test transactions, 50 of them fraud. The rule that always answers "no fraud" finds none of the frauds and still scores 0.990; the logistic regression finds 5 of 50 and scores 0.991. Almost every dot is a legitimate transaction, which is why accuracy hides the failure.
alt: Two grids of 5000 dots, mostly grey, with 50 frauds marked in red. In the first none is found; in the second 5 are found.

anchor: ## 2. Three sets, three jobs
caption: Figure 4.2 — Three sets, three jobs. The training set (341 rows) is for fitting and tuning, the validation set (114 rows) is for decisions that need unseen data such as the threshold, and the test set (114 rows) is opened once at the end.
alt: Three cards side by side: training set for fitting and tuning, validation set for choosing the threshold, test set for the final score, the last one marked as locked away until the end.

anchor: ## 4. The confusion matrix and what to read from it
caption: Figure 4.3 — The four boxes of the confusion matrix, with what each kind of error costs in the cancer problem. A missed malignant case is the costly mistake; a false alarm costs extra tests.
alt: A two-by-two grid: true positive, false negative, false positive and true negative, each with a short note on what it means and costs.

anchor: ## The protocol, in order
caption: Figure 4.6 — The protocol as a one-way track: tune the hyperparameter (C = 1), choose the threshold (0.463), lock everything, then score the test set once. There is no arrow back; going back would turn the test set into a second validation set.
alt: Four boxes in a row joined by forward arrows: tune, choose the threshold, lock, test once, with a note that nothing found at the last step sends you back.

anchor: On the 114 test cases the model finds 38 of the 42
caption: Figure 4.5 — The 42 malignant test cases as dots. With so few, one case is worth about 2.4 points of recall, so missing four rather than two moves the number a long way.
alt: 42 dots in two rows; most are filled green for found cases and the last four are red rings for missed cases.

anchor: A stated target (95% of malignant cases found) says what we want
caption: Figure 4.4 — The model's validation scores for the 71 benign and the 43 malignant cases, with the default threshold 0.5 and the chosen 0.463. Almost every case sits at one end or the other; the two malignant cases that fall below 0.463 are the ones the chosen threshold still misses.
alt: Two overlapping histograms of validation scores from zero to one: benign cases piled near zero, malignant cases piled near one, with vertical lines at 0.5 and 0.463 and a few malignant cases left of the lines.

anchor: ## 3. The result
caption: Figure 5.2 — How one point's silhouette is built. It compares the average distance to its own group, a(i), with the average distance to the nearest other group, b(i). The score for the whole clustering in this session, 0.757, is the average over all points. The drawing is a diagram of the construction, not the notebook's data.
alt: Two cluster regions with one orange point inside the left one; arrows run from it to points in its own cluster (labelled a) and to points in the other cluster (labelled b).

anchor: A tangle in the 2D map doesn't prove that the digits
caption: Figure 5.3 — PCA as a shadow, on a case small enough to see: Session 0's 150 iris flowers, two measurements each (petal length and petal width). The first principal direction is the line along which the flowers vary most; each flower's shadow on it is its first component, and the shadows keep most of the spread.
alt: A scatter of iris petal length against petal width with a long diagonal line through the cloud and short segments from each point to its nearest point on the line.

anchor: The clusters group digits that *look alike in pixel space*
caption: Figure 5.4 — Top: one real 8×8 digit of each kind from the data. Bottom: the 10 k-means cluster centres drawn as 8×8 images, each with the digits that make up most of its cluster. A centre is an average image, so a cluster that mixes digits has a blurred centre.
alt: A row of ten real 8 by 8 digit images and below it ten blurred cluster-centre images with the digits that dominate each cluster.

anchor: This loop is old: Stuart Lloyd described it
caption: Figure 5.1 — The same updates as above, one panel each, with the path every centre takes. A hollow circle is where a centre was, a cross is where the update moves it, and the line between them is the move. The title of each panel gives the sum of squared distances from every point to its nearest centre before and after the update. It never goes up, and in the third update nothing moves, which is why k-means stops.
alt: Three scatter panels of the same 600 points coloured by cluster, each with four hollow circles joined by lines to crosses that mark where the cluster centres move in that update.

anchor: From this session on, the course builds its networks
caption: Figure 6.1 — One unit. Each input is multiplied by its own weight, the products are added together with a bias, and an activation function turns the sum into the unit's output. Logistic regression is one such unit with a sigmoid activation.
alt: Three input circles with arrows labelled by weights into an adding box that also receives a bias, followed by an activation box and an output.

anchor: ## 2. Why layers need a non-linear step
caption: Figure 6.2 — Two linear layers collapse into one. The chain W₁ then W₂ gives the same output (-4.61296337) as a single layer with weights W₂W₁ and bias W₂b₁ + b₂, so a straight boundary stays straight.
alt: Two rows. Top: input through layer one and layer two to an output. Bottom: input through one merged layer to the same output value.

anchor: ## 4. How a model learns: a loss, a gradient and a small step
caption: Figure 6.4 — The training loop that every fit hides. Compute predictions, measure the loss, compute the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight, take a small step against it, and go round again.
alt: Four boxes arranged in a cycle: forward pass, loss, gradient, step, with arrows running clockwise and a note to repeat until the loss stops falling.

anchor: Backpropagation was popularised in 1986
caption: Figure 6.6 — Backpropagation on the one-unit model. Forward, the loss is computed from the weights through the scores and the probabilities. Backward, the chain rule carries the gradient from the loss back to the weights: [-0.34001, -0.473045] for the weights and -0.002774 for the bias, the same numbers as the formula by hand.
alt: A row of four boxes (weights, scores, probabilities, loss) with forward arrows above and red backward arrows below ending at the weights, labelled with the gradient values.

anchor: ## 5. A network that learns XOR
caption: Figure 6.7 — The network that learns XOR: two inputs, four tanh units and one sigmoid output. Counting the weights and biases layer by layer gives 17 numbers to learn.
alt: A network diagram with two input circles, four hidden circles and one output circle, joined by lines, annotated with the parameter counts of each layer and a total of 17.

anchor: This is what hidden layers do: they turn the inputs into new features
caption: Figure 6.3 — The hand-built XOR network, drawn two ways. Left: each hidden unit is one straight line across the square of inputs (solid: at least one input on; dashed: both on). Right: the same four points described by the two hidden units' answers. In these new coordinates one straight line separates the two classes, which no line could do on the left.
alt: Left: the unit square with the four XOR points and two parallel diagonal lines. Right: the four points redrawn with the two hidden answers as axes, and one diagonal line with the two class-one points on one side and the two class-zero points on the other.

anchor: Nothing in the loop knows about flowers
caption: Figure 6.5 — The loss as a landscape over the two weights (the bias held at 0 for the contours), with the real path of the 100 gradient steps from the starting guess [1.5, −1.5]. The path crosses the contours toward lower loss; the dots, one every 10 steps, bunch up as the slope flattens.
alt: Contour lines of the loss over the first and second weight, with a dotted path of 100 points that starts at the upper-left start and curves down to the minimum on the right.

anchor: ### The same three runs as pictures
caption: Figure 7.1 — A lookup card for reading training curves. Each row shows the real curves from this session's three runs, what to notice in them, what it means, and what to try first. The same order doubles as a debugging checklist.
alt: A table of three rows. Each row has a thumbnail of one run's loss curves, a description of the pattern, the diagnosis (too simple, too flexible, steps too big) and the first fix to try.

anchor: ## 3. Fixing overfitting, one change at a time
caption: Figure 7.4 — Dropout. At each training step about half of the hidden units are switched off, a different set each time, so the network cannot rely on any single one. At prediction time all units are on.
alt: Two copies of the same small network. In each, two of the four hidden units are crossed out; the crossed-out units differ between the two steps.

anchor: ## 4. When the curves look fine but the model is broken
caption: Figure 7.5 — The softmax bug on ten training points. With a sigmoid on each row, every prediction is its own probability and they match the labels (accuracy 100%). With softmax taken down the batch, the ten predictions share one unit of probability, so every one is below 0.5 and the model says 0 for all of them (accuracy 50%).
alt: Two bar charts of ten predictions. Left, the sigmoid output: bars at 1 or 0 matching the true labels. Right, the softmax-over-the-batch output: all bars at 0.2 or below, all under the 0.5 line.

anchor: Run C can only draw a straight line, so it cuts through both moons
caption: Figure 7.2 — Why run B's loss is so large. Left: its validation predictions are almost all at 0 or 1, so when one is wrong it is wrong with total confidence. Right: the loss for a single example whose true label is 1, against the probability the model gave it. The curve rises without limit as the probability falls, until PyTorch's `BCELoss` caps it at 100.
alt: Left, a histogram of run B's validation predictions with almost all of them at zero or one. Right, a curve of loss against predicted probability on a log axis rising steeply to a flat cap at 100.

anchor: - **0.0001** is safe but slow.
caption: Figure 7.3 — Learning rate on a real loss, the single sigmoid unit of Session 6 on versicolor and virginica, from its starting guess. Left: the loss at the point reached by one step of each size along the first downhill direction, with the three rates marked. Right: the loss after each step for the same three rates. A tiny rate barely moves; a good one descends; a huge one jumps past the valley, lands higher than it started, and descends again from the far side.
alt: Left, a curve of loss along a line with a low valley and three markers: one near the start, one near the valley, one far beyond it. Right, three loss curves over steps: slow descent, fast descent, and a curve that jumps up first and descends slowly.

anchor: ## 3. Counting parameters
caption: Figure 8.2 — The CNN as a stack of blocks, with the shape of what comes out of each. The same small filters are reused at every position, so the whole network has 12,810 parameters; the dense network on the same image has 101,770.
alt: A row of boxes from the 1 by 28 by 28 image through two convolution and two max-pooling blocks to a linear layer of 10 scores, with parameter counts, above a smaller diagram of the dense network with 101,770 parameters.

anchor: ## 2. A convolution, computed by hand
caption: Figure 8.1 — One convolution step with real numbers. A 3×3 patch of the first training digit (boxed, left) is multiplied cell by cell with the vertical-edge filter, and the nine products are added into one number: one pixel of the feature map.
alt: The digit with a small box on its edge, then three 3 by 3 grids of numbers: the patch of pixel values, the filter, and their cell-by-cell products with the sum of the products.

anchor: a gap of 4 points on a dataset where both do well doesn't tell us much
caption: Figure 8.3 — What each network learned to look at. Top: four of the dense network's 128 hidden units, each drawn as its 784 weights arranged as the 28×28 image they connect to; every unit has its own weight for every pixel. Bottom: the CNN's 16 learned filters, each only nine weights, used at every position.
alt: Top, four noisy 28 by 28 weight images from the dense network. Bottom, sixteen small 3 by 3 filters from the convolutional network.

anchor: a gap of 4 points on a dataset where both do well doesn't tell us much
caption: Figure 8.4 — The CNN's first layer on one digit. Top: the 16 filters it learned. Bottom: the 16 feature maps they produce for the first training digit, after the ReLU. Each map lights up where its own filter's pattern occurs, a stroke direction or an edge.
alt: A row of 16 small learned filters and below it 16 feature maps of one digit, each highlighting different strokes.

anchor: ## 2. One split, made by file
caption: Figure 9.1 — Two ways to build the sets. Splitting the list of file names once gives each photo one job (1400 training, 300 validation, 300 test, none shared). Reshuffling the stream on every pass can hand the same photo to validation on one pass and to test on another, so the test score stops being a fair measure.
alt: Left, a list of photo files split once into training, validation and test boxes. Right, a stream reshuffled on each pass, where coloured validation and test squares land on different photos each pass and can overlap.

anchor: ## 4. Backbone and head
caption: Figure 9.2 — The same backbone and head in three versions. From scratch trains everything (2,230,277 parameters); frozen features locks the pretrained backbone and trains only the head (6,405); fine-tuning unlocks the last 4 of the 19 blocks as well (1,532,485).
alt: Three rows of 19 blocks followed by a head. In the first row every block is coloured as trained; in the second all backbone blocks are grey and locked; in the third the first 15 are grey and the last 4 coloured.

anchor: **Run 2: frozen features.**
caption: Figure 9.3 — What the frozen backbone sees. Each dot is one of the 300 test photos, coloured by flower and flattened to two dimensions by PCA. Left: from the raw pixels, the colours are mixed together. Right: from the 1,280 numbers the frozen ImageNet backbone computes per photo, the kinds start to separate, with tulips and roses mostly on the left and daisies and dandelions mostly on the right, although two dimensions still leave a lot of overlap. No flower label was used to build either map.
alt: Two scatter plots of 300 test photos coloured by flower type: a tangled cloud from raw pixels, and clearly separated groups from the frozen backbone's features.

anchor: The confusion matrix for the fine-tuned model shows 265 of 300 test photos correct
caption: Figure 9.4 — Every test photo the fine-tuned model got wrong, with its true flower and what the model said. The 35 mistakes include the rose and tulip photos the text discusses; several are photos where the flower is small, partly hidden or not the main subject.
alt: A grid of 35 small flower photos, each titled with the true flower and the model's wrong answer.

anchor: ## 2. Tokens and ids
caption: Figure 10.1 — From text to numbers in three steps: split into tokens, give each token an id, and let each id pick a row of learned numbers. The ids 5, 3, 6, 4, 2, 1, 0 are labels, not quantities.
alt: The sentence 'The movie was not good at all' split into seven word tokens, each with its id, and each id pointing to one row of an embedding table.

anchor: ## 3. Counting words: TF-IDF
caption: Figure 10.2 — A bag of words records which words appear and how often, not their order, so "not good" and "good not" give identical counts. A word pair is a feature of its own, which is what the bigram model adds.
alt: Two orderings of the words 'not' and 'good' both point to the same bag of words with a count of one for each word.

anchor: ## 4. Reading in order: an LSTM
caption: Figure 10.4 — An LSTM reads a review one token at a time, passing its memory from step to step; the last memory feeds the output score. In a batch, short reviews are padded to a common length, and packing lets the LSTM skip the padding.
alt: Five LSTM boxes in a row, one per token of 'the movie was not good', with the memory passed from each to the next and ending in a score. Below, a batch of three reviews of different lengths with padding shown as empty cells.

anchor: ## 5. Probing with sentences
caption: Figure 10.5 — Six hand-written sentences scored by the three models. "Not good" pulls the word-pair model down the most; none of the models handles "not bad"; the LSTM barely reacts to "not".
alt: Dot chart with six sentences as rows and three dots per row, one per model, showing the probability of a positive review from 0 to 1.

anchor: A single-word model gives "good" a positive weight (1.49)
caption: Figure 10.3 — The 12 most positive and 12 most negative weights of the word-pair model. Single words are blue and word pairs are orange; the weights read as evidence for a positive review (right) or a negative one (left). Single words dominate the extremes; the only two pairs that make the list are "the best" and "the worst".
alt: A horizontal bar chart of the 12 most negative and 12 most positive features of the word-pair logistic regression, coloured by whether each is a single word or a pair.

anchor: The embedding layer's 32-number vectors were learned from the reviews alone
caption: Figure 10.6 — A flat map of some learned 32-number word vectors: four words from the text (large, bold) and their six nearest neighbours each, flattened to two dimensions by PCA. Words the LSTM treats alike sit near each other; the map is an approximation, because 32 dimensions cannot be drawn exactly in 2.
alt: A scatter of word labels in four colours, one colour per focus word, with the focus words in bold and their nearest neighbours around them.

anchor: The picture shows the same table as a heatmap.
caption: Figure 11.1 — Attention for the word "it". Its query is matched against every token's key; the match scores become weights (0.59 to battery, 0.22 to empty, much less to the rest) that are drawn as line widths; the new vector for "it" is the weighted mix of the values, [0.12, 0.81].
alt: The word 'it' on the left sends lines of different thickness to five key boxes (robot, battery, because, it, empty); each key has a value vector, and the values are mixed into a new vector for 'it' on the right.

anchor: The picture shows the same table as a heatmap.
caption: Figure 11.2 — The same computation as matrix shapes. Queries times transposed keys give a 5 × 5 table of scores; a softmax along each row turns it into weights; the weights times the values give one new vector per token.
alt: Matrix multiplication diagram: Q (5 by 3) times K transposed (3 by 5) gives scores (5 by 5); softmax gives weights (5 by 5); weights times V (5 by 2) gives the output (5 by 2).

anchor: In the table, *robot* attends only to itself
caption: Figure 11.3 — The attention weights without and with the causal mask. With the mask, every token reads only itself and the tokens before it, so the cells above the diagonal become zero and each row is shared among fewer tokens: "it" now gives 0.76 to battery, against 0.59 before.
alt: Two five-by-five tables of attention weights over the tokens robot, battery, because, it, empty. The left one is full; the right one has dots above the diagonal and larger weights in the remaining cells.

anchor: ## 4. Tokens are not always words
caption: Figure 11.5 — Four words as BERT's subword tokens. A common word is one token; "tokenization" is two (ids 19204 and 3989); rare or invented words are cut into several pieces from a vocabulary of 30,522, so nothing is ever unknown.
alt: Four rows of coloured chips: 'battery' as one chip, 'unbelievably' as five, 'tokenization' as two and 'Zorblatt-9000' as seven.

anchor: The table summarises it. Averaged over all 144 heads
caption: Figure 11.4 — All 144 attention heads of BERT, 12 layers by 12 heads, each cell showing how much "it" attends to "battery", for the sentence ending in "empty" (left) and in "broken" (right). Most heads give it little: only 14 (left) and 20 (right) of the 144 give it more than 0.1, and the red squares mark the strongest head in each sentence. Picking the strongest of 144 is searching for a best case.
alt: Two 12 by 12 heatmaps of attention weight from the word it to the word battery across 12 layers and 12 heads: mostly pale, with a few dark cells and a red square on the darkest one in each.

anchor: The prompt is 35 tokens. The chat template wraps
caption: Figure 12.1 — The loop a language model runs to write an answer. Each pass produces probabilities for every token in the vocabulary, one token is picked and appended, and the loop repeats until the end-of-turn token is picked.
alt: Flow diagram: tokens so far go into the model, which outputs a probability for every token; one token is picked and appended to the tokens so far, and the loop repeats until the end-of-turn token is picked.

anchor: Now the same question with a defence we might expect to help.
caption: Figure 12.7 — The whole system, with the injection path in red. A document that carries hidden instructions is retrieved with the real one, lands inside the prompt, and the model follows it; only the check outside the model stops it.
alt: System diagram: question, retriever, score gate with an abstain branch, prompt, model, output check, answer. A red dashed path shows a forum post with hidden instructions entering through the retriever into the prompt, the model obeying it, and the output check blocking the result.

anchor: ## 3. Measuring the retriever by itself
caption: Figure 12.6 — The best retrieval score for each of the twelve questions. Every question with an answer scores 0.301 or more; every question without one scores 0.26 or less. The threshold of 0.28 sits in the gap.

anchor: With a warning in the prompt (the context is untrusted data
